newsitem.title: MALI: Chaos as Mali kicks off 2nd multiparty polls.
newsitem.headline: Chaos as Mali kicks off 2nd multiparty polls.

text.p: Chaos marred the start of Mali's second multi-party national elections on Sunday with widespread organisational problems disrupting polling for a new national assembly.

Sunday's parliamentary poll, a May presidential election and a June municipal election are a test of how deeply democracy has taken root in the West African nation, widely praised for its 1992 democratic transition.

But lack of voting materials, differences in details on voter cards and on voting lists and names missing from the lists frustrated many voters' efforts to cast their ballots for the new 147-seat national assembly.

"We have fallen behind schedule because of numerous logistical problems and we are obliged to extend polling," Lawyer Mamadou Dante, a member of the independent national electoral commission (CENI), told Reuters.
Many polling stations in the capital failed to open at 8 a.m. as planned. State radio correspondents reported similar problems outside the capital. Polling had been due to end at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT).

A total 1,500 candidates from 21 parties contested the election. Most were supporters of civilian President Alpha Oumar Konare, a historian elected in 1992, or candidates from two main opposition alliances.
The two alliances, in a pre-poll statement, denounced preparations for the poll.
"Conditions do not exist for the Malian people to express themselves freely," the opposition Front for Change and Democracy (FCD) and the Rally of Patriotic Forces (RFP) said.
They cited problems with voter cards and electoral lists.
The Commission, set up in January by Konare at the demand of the opposition, said voters without polling cards could use identity cards if they were on voter lists.
The RFP includes supporters of the former single party and jailed former dictator Moussa Traore, whose 1991 overthrow cleared the way for democratic reform.
The FCD portrays itself as heir to the tradition of independence leader Modibo Keita, a nationalist and hardline socialist who declared a one-party state after independence from France in 1960.
Konare faces nine challengers in a May 4 presidential poll. He has steered Mali on a course of economic liberalisation, winning praise from the United States and the World Bank.

James Wolfensohn began his first foreign trip as World Bank president in Mali in 1995 and a year later the-then U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher singled out Mali as the first stop of his own first African tour.
Landlocked on the edge of the Sahara desert, Mali has few natural advantages apart from gold -- a sector it is expanding.
Konare sealed a peace deal last year in a revolt by light-skinned Tuaregs in the north, who took up arms in 1990 denouncing domination by majority blacks from the south.
Five million Malians were eligible to vote on Sunday. A dozen poll observers from Germany, Canada, Britain and the Netherlands monitored polling.
First results were unlikely before a couple of days. The constitutional court will announce final results. Any runoffs will take place on April 27.
